chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad ibn Uthman who said:
I heard him (peace be upon him) saying: 'Verily, supplication repels the decree and breaks it, just as the thread is broken, even though it has been twirled firmly.'

key_terms.أُبرم: Ubrim — was made firm/finalized; from ibram (إبرام), to twist/finalize firmly
key_terms.الدعاء: Du'a (supplication) — directed personal prayer addressed to God, distinct from ritual salat
key_terms.السلك: Al-silk — thread, rope, or cord; here metaphorically for a firm, twirled decree
key_terms.القضاء: Al-Qada' — Divine decree/ordinance; the determined divine will regarding specific events
key_terms.ينقضه: Yanquduhu — breaks/unravels it; from naqdh (نقض), to undo, reverse, annul

ai.seo_question: Can supplication (dua) repel or change divine decree in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) teaches through a vivid simile that supplication (du'a) has the power to avert even firmly-established divine decrees. This hadith addresses a core theological question about the relationship between human prayer and divine predetermination in Shia thought. The audience of early Shia Muslims would have understood 'al-qada'' (the decree) as referring to God's determined ordinances, while the imagery of a rope being unraveled — even after being firmly twisted — emphasizes that no decree is beyond the power of sincere supplication to alter.
